column4: Compliance of PNRI to Environmental Laws and Regulations: Implementation of the Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) Management Plan and Chemical and Hazardous Waste Management
column6:
The Philippine Nuclear Research Institute (PNRI) envisions to be an institution of excellence in nuclear science and technology propelled by a dynamic and committed workforce in the mainstream of national development. To succeed, contribution of the Institute to the improvement of the quality of the Filipino life must be through the highest standards of nuclear research and development, specialized nuclear services, nuclear technology transfer, and effective and efficient implementation of nuclear safety practices and regulations. However, PNRI should also address the potential impacts of its activities on the environment. Thereby, compliance with the existing Philippine Environmental Policy (PD No. 1151, 1957) and Philippine Environmental Code (PD No. 1152, 1977) is required, as well as compliance with ISO 17025 which is the standard for testing and calibration services. 

Currently, PNRI is currently housing a decommissioned transformer containing Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCB) and approximately 200L of pure PCB oil. Philippines as a member party of the of Stockholm Convention on “Protecting human health and the environment from POPs”, agreed that they can no longer produce PCBs and are obliged to stop using this chemical due to its adverse health effects to humans and animals. The Philippine government committed that by March 2014 Philippines will phase-out the use of PCB. However, due to large number of institutions that uses PCB, the Philippine government extended its deadline to December 2018 or at the earliest possible time. In line with this commitment by the government, the possessed PCB equipment and waste of PNRI must be disposed of immediately.

Additionally, PNRI as a research institute generates hazardous waste as an inherent byproduct of ongoing scientific procedures and laboratory activities. Proper and continuous treatment and disposal of hazardous waste must be done in accordance with DAO 2013-22 "Revised Procedures and Standards for the Management of Hazardous Wastes". Additionally, ISO 17025 specifies that laboratories must establish a procedure for the disposal of test or calibration items, ensuring that all necessary measures are taken to protect the integrity of the tests and calibration performed. Therefore, establishment of a comprehensive and rigorous hazardous waste management program and disposal is imperative to ensure that PNRI is in compliance with safety standards, ensures all provisions necessary to avoid contamination and deterioration, and mitigates potential health and environmental risks.

column4: Muslim Filipinos' Registry: Advocacy and Educational Campaign and Mobile Registration
column6:
This project is in collaboration with Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA). Under Rule IV, Section 10 (p) of the IRR of R.A. 9997, NCMF shall assist the National Statistics Office (NSO), now Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), in conducting a census on the actual population of Muslim Filipinos in the country. Hence, this proposal intends to provide the most detailed information on the numbers and data of Muslim Filipinos, its territorial spread, socio-demographic and professional structures, and the socio-economic specificity of households and families, as well as their resources and dwelling needs. Aside from the census, NCMF shall also undertake to assist PSA in its various programs and services, thus Muslim Filipinos will equally enjoy the services rendered by the government to the Filipinos.

In 2024, the Commission was endorsed by the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) which was approved by the Department of Budget and Management (DBM), thus, allocated funds amounting to six (6) million for the advocacy campaign and mobile registration programs which will be implemented for FY 2025. This covers sixty (60) Muslim community areas across the country wherein five (5) areas will be served by each of the regional offices. The NCMF is targeting to cover the whole regions in the country so that no one should be left behind. Hence, the NCMF is enhancing the budgetary requirements of the previous approved budget that was allocated to NCMF for the said programs in order to effectively and properly implement the said program.

To sustain these noteworthy initiatives and aim to reach out all Muslim communities across the country in order to capture the accurate and conclusive number of population of Muslim Filipinos with the goal of “NO ONE SHOULD BE LEFT BEHIND”.

Thus, the NCMF is intending to conduct the following:

Geographical and Accessibility Challenges. In more remote areas, particularly in Mindanao where many Muslim Filipinos live, access to government services, including vital statistics registration, can be limited. Poor infrastructure, lack of transportation, and the distance to registration offices can make it difficult for people to register vital events.

Cultural and Religious Factors. In some Muslim communities, traditional practices and religious customs may take precedence over formal government processes. In certain cases, Islamic marriage or birth rituals may not be immediately followed by official registration with the government. Some may not prioritize formal registration because they view their religious or community-based documentation as sufficient.

Lack of Awareness. There might be a lack of awareness about the importance of registering vital statistics or about the processes involved. If communities do not have enough information on how to register or the benefits of having official documents, they may not see the need to do so.

Political and Social Issues. In some areas, Muslim communities may feel a sense of alienation from the central government due to historical or ongoing political tensions. This distrust may discourage people from engaging with government institutions, including registration processes.

Bureaucratic Difficulties. Sometimes, the process of registering vital statistics can be complicated or require documents that some people may not have access to, such as identification or proof of residency. These bureaucratic hurdles can deter people from completing the registration process.

To capture unregistered Muslim Filipinos and improve registration rates in the identified communities and raise awareness about the importance of registering vital statistics and the benefits it provides, and provide a venue where they can conveniently register their vital events, all regional and provincial offices shall have a convergence program in coordination and partnership with PSA, LGUs, Muslim Community Leaders, and other stakeholders.

This community activity is in partnership with the Regional Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), Local Civil Registry Offices (LCROs), Shariah Offices and Shariah Counsellors, Local Government Units (LGUs) and Barangay LGUs. The proponents of this proposal may likewise ask for assistance to other institutions that have defined jurisdiction over the activities that the NCMF personnel want to conduct.

The NCMF Regional Offices and its provincial/field/satellite offices will implement the said activities. In any case, the Central Office through the Bureau of Muslim Settlement will supervise and monitor the activities and consolidate the reports from the regional and provincial/satellite offices.

COMPONENT PROGRAMS AND ACTIVITIES:

1. Planning and Coordination with stakeholders
Stakeholders’ Consultation/inter-agency meetings
a. Mapping
b. Focus Group Discussions

2. Advocacy and Educational Campaign Program

Conduct of awareness programs to Muslim communities to understand the importance of participating in the census of population, the benefits in availing civil and National ID registrations, process of securing authority to solemnize and other related programs are necessary to encourage them to cooperate for their own benefits. For the program to be gender responsive, lecture on “Anti-Child Marriage Law” is also included.

3. Mobile Registration

Bringing the services to the community is an effective way to capture every constituent that needs to be included in the program, especially areas that are not being reached by government services.

4. Evaluation, Assessment, and Validation of Report

In this activity, the regional and provincial sub-offices will present and submit their reports for evaluation, assessment and validation to ensure that the program implementation is effective and efficient. Evaluating the result and outcome of the program will help identify areas for improvement and will determine its relevance and sustainability to achieve the goal.

column4: FIBRECYCL: Facilitating Innovative Bottle Recycling for Eco-friendly Conversion into Yarn for Closed-Loop Production

the informal waste sector in the Philippines is estimated to include over 100,000 people who work to collect, sort, and sell waste. This includes families, women, and children who work on dumpsites or collect waste from households or garbage collectors. Sold at about P10 per kilogram in the form of as-collected bottles and almost P250 per kilogram in pellet form, polyester (PET) is an indispensable part of modern society. Hence, building the capacity to upcycle PET bottle waste into high-value input materials offers a promising instrument for economic development in The informal waste sector and a solution to environmental challenges that can be integrated into the Philippine Development Plan.

Furthermore, forging public-private partnerships with different stakeholders ensures that significant volume is achieved and quality assurance is maintained to establish a robust supply chain. column4: Strengthening Urban Planning through Urban Carrying Capacity Assessment (SUP-UCCA)
column5: Department of Economy, Planning, and Development
column6:
This project is designed to include capacity-building activities, stakeholder collaboration, including possible means to institutionalize the conduct of urban carrying capacity assessments. This will help ensure that highly urbanized cities are better prepared to manage growth, infrastructure demands, and environmental sustainability. Ultimately, this will contribute in making more livable and resilient urban environments. For the first year (2026), the manual will be pilot-tested in four HUCs: Olongapo City, Zambales; San Juan City, Metro Manila; Lapu-lapu City, Cebu; and Iligan City, Lanao del Norte. They were selected because they are lowest ranking among HUCs in DTI's Cities and Municipalities Competitiveness Index (CMCI) in 2023. For the second year, we will be rolling out the manual in the remaining 29 HUCs and selected independent component cities, if feasible, through clustered sessions per major island group.

Target participants for the pilot-testing will include DEPDev Regional Offices (DROs), local planners from the identified HUCs, and relevant regional line agencies such as the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), and Department of Human Settlements and Urban Development (DHSUD).DEPDev will also create a project Inter-Staff Group (ISG), which will serve as a venue for technical discussions on the multi-sectoral scope of UCCA and further enhance the relevance and applicability of the UCCA Manual based on the results and lessons from its pilot testing in the target HUCs. The ISG will be headed by ANRES as lead implementing staff, and joined by technical personnel from Regional Development Staff (RDS), Infrastructure Staff (IS), Social Development Staff (SDS), and selected DROs.

column4: Construction of MSU-General Santos Center for Hydrology, Limnology, and Aquaculture in the Municipality of Lake Sebu, South Cotabato
column6:
The establishment of the MSU General Santos Center for Hydrology, Limnology, and Aquaculture represents a strategic response to the growing environmental and socio-economic challenges facing Lake Sebu in South Cotabato. Once a vital freshwater ecosystem and cultural stronghold for indigenous communities, the lake is now increasingly threatened by ecological degradation—characterized by recurring fish kills, foul odors, and high turbidity due to watershed deterioration, climate variability, and unsustainable aquaculture practices. The proposed one-story lakefront center will function as a multidisciplinary hub dedicated to applied scientific research, real-time hydrological and ecological monitoring, sustainable aquaculture development, and community-centered training programs. By integrating scientific expertise with indigenous knowledge systems, the initiative aims to support lake rehabilitation, strengthen climate resilience, and foster inclusive and science-based environmental governance.

Aligned with key Sustainable Development Goals—including SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), SDG 13 (Climate Action), SDG 14 (Life Below Water), SDG 15 (Life on Land), SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities), and SDG 17 (Partnerships for the Goals)—the project underscores MSU General Santos’s commitment to harmonizing development and environmental stewardship. Beyond serving as a research facility, the center will become a symbol of collective responsibility and collaboration, ensuring the long-term protection and sustainable management of one of Mindanao’s most important natural assets.

column4: Strengthening Resilience for Central Museum Buildings
column6:
The project, "Strengthening Resilience for Central Museum Buildings", is an initiative of the NMP under its Museum Development, Exhibition and Fit-Out Program. column4: Provision of Research and Development Support to the Horticulture Program of Asenso Global Gardens
column5: Northwestern Mindanao State College of Science and Technology
column6:
The Asenso Global Gardens (AGG) in Hoyohoy, Tangub City has emerged as a flagship destination for floral tourism, ornamental horticulture, and landscape innovation, drawing inspiration from globally themed gardens. With its increasing popularity and strategic role in the city’s agri-tourism initiatives, AGG has become more than just a showcase of beauty it is a platform for education, conservation, livelihood, and sustainable development.

However, to fully realize its potential as a center for excellence in horticulture, there is a need to embed systematic and science-based research and development (R&D) into its operations. Currently, AGG’s horticultural efforts rely heavily on traditional practices and aesthetic design principles. Without structured R&D support, opportunities for innovation, plant health management, sustainability, and long-term improvement may be missed.

This project addresses that gap by providing dedicated R&D support to the horticulture program of AGG. Through research collaborations, knowledge generation, technical training, and the application of horticultural science, the project will help transform AGG into a living laboratory for students, researchers, garden professionals, and policymakers. column4: MASAGANANG BUKID: Farmer-Led Sustainable Agriculture and Livelihood Enhancement in Northern Mindanao
column5: University of Science and Technology of Southern Philippines
column6:
The MASAGANANG BUKID project empowers local farmers by revitalizing traditional and sustainable farming practices that reduce input costs, improve soil health, and increase yield. Anchored on SDG 1 (No Poverty), SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), and SDG 13 (Climate Action), the project supports farmers with hands-on training, farm tools, organic inputs, post-harvest activities and cooperative-led marketing systems—all without the need for mobile devices or digital literacy.
It aims to strengthen existing farmer groups and cooperatives by equipping them with resources and knowledge on composting, seed banking, natural pest management, crop rotation, and low-cost post-harvest techniques. A farm-to-community market model will be established, using barangay-based collection points and farmer associations to reduce middlemen and transportation costs.
The project will benefit 1,200 smallholder farmers across Northern Mindanao, prioritizing those in GIDA, IP, and poverty-affected barangays.

column4: Construction of Campus Water System
column5: Cotabato Foundation College of Science and Technology
column6:
The project entails the construction of a comprehensive Campus Water System designed to provide a reliable and uninterrupted supply of clean and safe water to all facilities within the institution. This includes the development of water reservoirs that will serve as primary storage structures, ensuring adequate water volume during peak demand and emergencies. These reservoirs will be complemented by a strategically engineered network of pipes that will transport water efficiently from the source to the storage facilities and subsequently to various campus buildings.

column4: Design and Build Scheme of Wastewater Treatment Facility for DENR, EMB, and MGB ROs of EMB-R10
column6:
The project involves the design and construction of a compact wastewater treatment facility within the DENR-X compound to manage all wastewater generated from offices and laboratories. The facility will cover an estimated 200 square meters and will utilize biological, chemical, and physical treatment processes.
It will be implemented through a Design and Build Scheme pursuant to Republic Act No. 12009 (New Government Procurement Act) and its forthcoming Implementing Rules and Regulations (IRR). This modality integrates both design and construction under one contract to ensure efficiency, accountability, and project quality.

Treatment Process Overview
The WWTF will include the following major components:
● Sump Pit: Serves as the holding and flow control structure for incoming wastewater.
● Primary and Secondary Screens: Remove solid particles and debris.
● Oil and Water Separator: Eliminates oil and grease content.
● Sequencing Batch Reactor (SBR): Provides biological treatment using aeration and settling cycles.
● Coagulation and Flocculation Tanks: Treat laboratory effluents with chemical coagulants and flocculants.
● Final Settling and Disinfection Tanks: Clarify effluent and disinfect pathogens before discharge.
● Effluent Tank: Holds treated wastewater prior to disposal compliant with DAO 2016-08.

Discharges from the facility will meet the General Effluent Standards (GES) for Class SC waters, protecting Macajalar Bay and surrounding waterways.
 Implementation will proceed in four phases:
1. Preliminary Study – Preparation of project scope, budget, and preliminary design; securing necessary permits and clearances.
2. Design and Engineering – Preparation and submission of detailed engineering designs, environmental impact assessment report, value engineering analysis, and cost estimates.
3. Construction and Installation – Construction of the treatment facility, support structures, drainage, access roads, electrical systems, and perimeter fence.
4. Testing and Commissioning – Performance verification to ensure compliance with regulatory standards and functionality of the treatment system.

Total Implementation Period: 300 calendar days from the issuance of the Notice to Proceed (NTP).
Total Project Cost: ₱20,000,000.00

column4: Real-time Water Quality Monitoring Equipment (WQME) of EMB-R10
column6:
Iligan Bay and Macajalar Bay are important coastal water bodies in Northern Mindanao which are both within a Water Quality Management Area (WQMA): the Iligan Bay-Misamis Oriental and Lanao del Norte WQMA by virtue of DENR Administrative Order No. 2025-02 for Iligan Bay; and Cagayan de Oro River Basin and Adjacent Rivers WQMA by virtue of DENR Administrative Order No. 2013-18; and Tagoloan River Basin WQMA by virtue of DENR Administrative Order No. 2016-16. These bays support fisheries, local livelihoods, marine biodiversity, and the communities of adjacent coastal cities/municipalities. The designation of a Water Quality Management Area as mandated thru RA 9275 otherwise known as the Clean Water Act of 2004 is a holistic national program on water quality management that is primarily developed as a tool in the abatement and control of pollution from land-based sources.
However, both bays have been experiencing environmental pressures from pollution, waste discharge, siltation, and other anthropogenic impacts:
• In Macajalar Bay (which receives discharges households channeled through creeks and rivers, urban/industrial runoff), fecal coliform data showed to be non-conforming from the DENR guidelines in the past five (5) years. However, a declining trend is observed in the fecal coliform monitoring data in most of the seven (7) rivers that exit to the bay, suggesting that interventions are showing positive outcomes.
• Pollution sources include domestic waste and sewage (especially from communities lacking proper sanitation or sewerage infrastructure), industrial discharges (factories, commercial areas), and effluents from animal raising (piggeries, poultry) along the coast. 
• Additionally, a study on the Riverine Microplastic Pollution: Insights from Cagayan de Oro River, Philippines (Gabriel, et al, June 2013) have documented significant microplastic pollution in waterways feeding into Macajalar Bay (e.g. surface water of the river that drains into the bay) — which indicates the accumulation of plastic litter and microplastics at or near the bay’s mouth.
• In Iligan Bay, particularly along Misamis Oriental and Lanao del Norte portions, regular monthly monitoring is took effect in CY 2025 following its designation as a WQMA, wherein 1st Semester-CY 2025 water sampling results of the bay revealed non-conformance mostly to fecal coliform guidelines for Classes “SA”, “SB”, and “SC” Waters set forth under DENR Administrative Order No. 2021-19, Updated Water Quality Guidelines and General Effluent Standards for Selected Parameters.
• A 2017 by SunStar report said that coastal degradation, particularly in Agutayan Island in Jasaan — such as siltation, pollution, and degradation of marine habitats (e.g., corals, seagrass beds) — threatens fisheries, biodiversity, tourism potential, and the health and welfare of coastal communities. 
Given these conditions — and recognizing that conventional monitoring (periodic manual sampling) may not sufficiently detect pollution events in time — there is a strong need for a continuous, real-time water quality monitoring system for these bays.

Moreover, recent research in the Philippines has shown the feasibility and value of using low-cost sensor-based or IoT-based systems for water quality monitoring, capable of delivering real-time data and alerting communities or authorities to contamination events.
 
Thus, this project seeks to deploy three (3) units real-time water quality monitoring equipment in Iligan Bay and Macajalar Bay — aimed at providing timely, accessible, continuous water quality data to support environmental protection, sustainable marine resource management, public health safety, and informed decision-making. Each unit of the Water Quality Monitoring Equipment (WQME) will cost approximately 5,500,000.00 on CY 2027, considering the influence to be contributed by inflation. Three (3) units of WQME will total to 16,500,000.00.

column4: Carrying Capacity and Population Dynamics: Effects and Opportunities for Sustainable Development in Highly Urbanized Areas in the Philippines (using Daytime and Nighttime Estimates)
column6:
Urbanization in the Philippines has accelerated rapidly in recent decades, leading to the expansion of highly urbanized areas (HUAs) that face mounting pressures on land, infrastructure, and natural resources. Local government units (LGUs) are challenged to balance population growth with sustainable urban development, ensuring that residents enjoy a good quality of life while avoiding irreversible environmental degradation.

The concept of Urban Carrying Capacity (UCC)—as defined in the Manual for the Conduct of Urban Carrying Capacity Assessment developed by Department of Economy, Planning, and Development’s (DEPDev)— provides a science-based framework to evaluate the maximum population size that an urban ecosystem can sustain without compromising environmental health, infrastructure efficiency, governance capacity, and public well-being. Unlike traditional planning approaches, UCC integrates limiting factors such as ecological conditions, infrastructure services, institutional governance, and public perception, making it a proactive tool for sustainable urban management.

In highly urbanized areas, population dynamics are not static. The distinction between daytime and nighttime populations is particularly relevant. Daytime populations often swell due to commuting workers, students, and visitors, placing additional stress on transportation systems, utilities, and public services. Nighttime populations, on the other hand, mainly reflect the resident base that relies on housing, sanitation, and community facilities. Assessing UCC through both daytime and nighttime estimates allows for a more nuanced understanding of urban pressures and resource demands.

This dual perspective highlights the effects of population fluctuations on carrying capacity and uncovers opportunities for sustainable development. By identifying when and how urban systems are most strained, program implementers, planners and policymakers can design targeted interventions—such as improved transport networks, equitable land use policies, and adaptive governance strategies—that enhance resilience and sustainability.

This study seeks to integrate the UCC assessment of DEPDev with existing indicators of population dynamics and CPD’s daytime and nighttime population estimates to determine the effects and opportunities for sustainable development in highly urbanized areas.

column4: Surigao del Norte Real-Time Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring System (CAAMS) Project
column5: Department of Environment and Natural Resources
column6:
Air quality monitoring is a vital tool for safeguarding environmental quality, protecting public health, and ensuring compliance with the Clean Air Act and its implementing rules and regulations. It plays a critical role in identifying sources of air pollution, tracking gas emissions, and supporting research and policy development.

Currently, the Province of Surigao del Norte lacks Continuous Ambient Air Quality Monitoring Stations (CAAQMS), creating a significant data gap in the Caraga Region’s environmental monitoring network. While previous initiatives have established monitoring stations in Butuan City and the Province of Agusan del Norte, Surigao del Norte remains without real-time air quality data. This is particularly concerning given the presence of major pollution sources, including the urban center of Surigao City and widespread mining operations throughout the province.

The absence of spatial coverage significantly limits the region’s capacity to effectively monitor and manage air quality. Without adequate monitoring infrastructure, it becomes difficult to measure local concentrations of Particulate Matter (PM2.5 and PM10), identify pollution hotspots in non-urban and emerging growth areas, and provide Local Government Units (LGUs) with reliable data necessary for implementing and planning under the Clean Air Act. This gap also hinders the timely issuance of public health advisories and impairs informed decision-making related to air quality. Ultimately, it prevents the development of a comprehensive understanding of the region’s overall air quality status.

To address these challenges, this project proposes the establishment of a network of three (3) state-of-the-art CAAQMS strategically located across Surigao del Norte. These stations will deliver real-time, continuous data on key air pollutants, including PM2.5, PM10, Sulfur Dioxide (SO₂), Nitrogen Oxides (NOₓ), Carbon Monoxide (CO), and Ozone (O₃), as well as rainfall data. The resulting information will enhance environmental governance, support evidence-based policymaking, and contribute to the protection of public health in the region.
